query: Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys have reported densities of 1.46–6 g/cm3 and commonly contain solid solutions together with intermetallic compounds. Earlier induction-melted Al–Mg-rich alloys established this structural complexity but did not resolve subsequent transformation pathways. Compositionally graded MgAlCuZnGd alloys showed region-dependent compression and corrosion performance, while studies of AlMgₓTiSnZn alloys associated Mg content with phase stability and multiple functional properties. Most prior work emphasized hardness and room-temperature compression, leaving corrosion, high-temperature oxidation, and evolution from metastable states comparatively underexplored. Within the design constraint of density below 6 g/cm3 and the tendency for constituent-property differences to promote stable intermetallic compounds, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain how a non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy evolves and why that evolution changes its corrosion and high-temperature oxidation behavior? Specify an unnamed controlled comparison, predictions relative to the initial baseline, boundary conditions, supporting prior observations, and an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: In non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloys, rapid solidification creates a metastable microstructure with nanoscale Mg‐rich regions that, upon modest thermal exposure, transform into stable Mg-bearing intermetallic compounds. This microstructural evolution promotes the in situ formation of protective Mg-Al oxide layers during high-temperature oxidation and alters local galvanic couples, thereby reducing corrosion rates compared to the as-cast state.
generation.material_initial_state: As-solidified alloy exhibiting a mixture of solid solution and metastable nanoscale Mg‐rich domains with minor intermetallic particles.
generation.intervention: A controlled post-solidification thermal exposure (e.g., moderate annealing below the melting point) to trigger the transformation of metastable domains into more stable intermetallic compounds.
generation.conditions: Experiments conducted at constant density (< 6 g/cm3), with samples exposed to identical corrosive (e.g., salt spray) and high-temperature oxidation environments; temperature and time parameters selected to allow transformation without full equilibrium.
generation.structural_mediator: The transformation and distribution of Mg-rich intermetallic compounds which mediate the formation of localized, protective Mg-Al oxide scales.
generation.mechanism: Thermal activation facilitates diffusion-driven phase separation of Mg from the supersaturated metastable matrix, resulting in formation of stable Mg-containing intermetallic phases. These phases act as preferential sites for the nucleation and growth of adherent, protective oxide layers. The altered interfacial chemistry reduces active corrosion sites and limits the oxidation rate by forming a continuous protective film.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the as-cast baseline, thermally treated alloys will exhibit a decrease in corrosion rates (e.g., via salt spray testing) and enhanced high-temperature oxidation resistance (e.g., lower oxidation weight gain) due to improved passivation by the protective oxide layers.
generation.baseline: The as-solidified non-equilibrium alloy containing metastable nanoscale Mg-rich domains and partially formed intermetallic compounds without a continuous protective oxide layer.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis is expected to hold under processing conditions that maintain density below 6 g/cm3 and under moderate thermal treatments that do not induce full homogenization or complete equilibrium microstructures.
generation.uncertainty: The exact intermetallic phases forming, their spatial distributions, and the detailed kinetics of the oxide layer development remain uncertain. Variation in alloy compositions and processing parameters could modify the evolution pathway and protective behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of the same Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy: one set is retained in the as-cast metastable state, and the other is subjected to a controlled annealing treatment. Expose both sets to identical corrosive environments (e.g., standardized salt spray test) and high-temperature oxidation conditions. Employ microstructural analysis (e.g., TEM/SEM) to verify intermetallic formation and surface oxide layers.
measurements: Corrosion rate (e.g., via mass loss or electrochemical impedance spectroscopy)
Oxidation weight gain over time at high temperature
Microstructural characterization (phase identification, oxide layer thickness, and continuity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not show a statistically significant decrease in corrosion rate and improved oxidation resistance compared to the as-cast baseline, or if microstructural analysis fails to indicate a meaningful transformation (i.e., no formation of stable Mg-bearing intermetallic compounds or protective oxide layers), then the hypothesis is falsified.
